questions.prompt: Salmonella typhimurium's invasins help it at THREE steps of infection. Which three?

options.text: Portal of entry, portal of exit, and transmission
Reservoir, transmission, and portal of entry
Avoiding defenses, toxin secretion, and siderophore release
Adherence, avoiding host defenses, and host damage

questions.explanation: Entering cells keeps it from being washed away, hides it from phagocytes and antibodies, and lets it lyse the cells.

why.A: Invasins don't decide entry, exit, or transmission.

questions.prompt: A nurse's unwashed hands carry bacteria from one patient's wound to the next patient. This is:

options.text: Direct contact, with the nurse acting as a passive carrier
Biological vector transmission, because the nurse is living
Vehicle transmission, because the hands moved the bacteria
Indirect contact, with the nurse's hands acting as a fomite

questions.explanation: Patient care is direct contact; a nurse who isn't infected but carries the microbe is a passive carrier (Module 18).

why.C: Hands moving bacteria during care is direct contact.

questions.prompt: Which pair shows the difference between a vehicle and a vector?

options.text: Contaminated well water vs a mosquito
A housefly vs an Anopheles mosquito
A sneeze at 0.5 m vs a cough at 3 m
A contaminated doorknob vs a cell phone

questions.explanation: Vehicles are non-living but move pathogens; vectors are living arthropods.

questions.prompt: A lab technician gets sick after a blood specimen splashes on her. How is this transmission classified?

options.text: Vehicle
Mechanical vector
Direct contact
Droplet

questions.explanation: The lecture classifies exposure to laboratory specimens as vehicle transmission.

questions.prompt: Which bacterium would most need IgA protease?

options.text: One that is injected parenterally deep into muscle by a contaminated needle
One that stays inside a biofilm on a tooth surface above the gum line
One that enters through a mucous membrane, like the gonorrhea bacterium
One that lives only on unbroken skin and never touches mucus at all

questions.explanation: IgA antibodies are most abundant in mucus, so mucosal invaders must destroy them.

why.A: Deep muscle has no mucus IgA.
why.B: Tooth surfaces above the gum aren't the IgA target.

questions.prompt: Which statement about host damage is FALSE?

options.text: Normal flora like Lactobacillus damage the host just as pathogens do.
Collagenase can contribute to gangrene.
Siderophores steal iron the host needs.
Salmonella damages cells by multiplying inside them until they lyse.
Host damage is what separates pathogens from normal flora.

questions.explanation: Normal flora go through reservoir, transmission, entry, adherence, and avoiding defenses — but they don't harm the host.

questions.prompt: Why were guinea pigs especially useful for detecting diphtheria toxin?

options.text: They are resistant to diphtheria bacteria
Their livers are poor at removing toxins
They make more IgA than other mammals
They can't develop immune responses

questions.explanation: Toxic effects show up clearly without the liver neutralizing them.

questions.prompt: A patient develops toxic shock syndrome with a very high fever and life-threatening low blood pressure. Which toxin type and organism fit?

options.text: Type II hemolysin from S. pyogenes
Type I superantigen from S. aureus
Endotoxin from S. aureus
Type III A-B toxin from C. botulinum

questions.explanation: Superantigens cause an excessive immune response.

why.C: S. aureus is Gram-positive, with no endotoxin.

questions.prompt: Why might a bacterium only become pathogenic after being infected by a bacteriophage?

options.text: Phages add a thick protein capsule that blocks phagocytosis
Phages destroy the bacterium's ribosomes, releasing toxins
Phages convert the bacterium's endotoxins into exotoxins
Prophage genes from lysogenic conversion can encode exotoxins

questions.explanation: Several exotoxins are encoded by prophage genes.

why.B: Phages don't destroy ribosomes to release toxins.

questions.prompt: Treating a Gram-negative bloodstream infection with an antibiotic that rapidly kills the bacteria can make a patient's fever spike. Why?

options.text: The antibiotic itself acts as a superantigen that overstimulates the immune system
The bacteria secrete extra exotoxin as they die, which raises the fever
Dying cells release endotoxin (LPS), triggering an excessive immune response
The antibiotic acts as a hemolysin, bursting red blood cells and raising fever

questions.explanation: Endotoxins are released when Gram-negative cells die and break apart.

questions.prompt: S. aureus walls itself inside a blood clot, but S. pyogenes dissolves a clot. Which statement explains both?

options.text: Coagulase and kinase both steal iron from red blood cells inside the clot
Both use coagulase to attract more WBCs to the site so they can be eaten
Both use kinase to feed on blood and grow faster inside the clot itself
Coagulase helps S. aureus hide from WBCs; kinase helps S. pyogenes escape them

questions.explanation: Both enzymes help avoid host defenses, in opposite ways.

questions.prompt: Which HAI prevention step most directly targets the 'compromised host' problem?

options.text: Using careful aseptic technique when handling lab specimens
Replacing the old term 'nosocomial' in hospital paperwork
Isolating burn patients away from infectious-disease patients
Teaching the public the plain-language term 'HAI' on posters

questions.explanation: Isolation keeps compromised hosts away from reservoirs.

questions.prompt: A UTI patient is told to drink lots of fluids. Which step of infection is this meant to work against?

options.text: Portal of exit
Adherence
Host damage
Reservoir

questions.explanation: Urine flow tries to wash away bacteria that haven't adhered.

why.A: Fluids flush; they don't target exit.

questions.prompt: Describe the three types of exotoxins, how each damages the host, and one example each.
questions.explanation: Type I superantigens cause an excessive immune response (S. aureus, toxic shock syndrome). Type II hemolysins lyse red blood cells (S. pyogenes). Type III A-B toxins: B binds the host cell and A inhibits protein synthesis or acts as a neurotoxin (C. botulinum, botulism/Botox).

questions.prompt: List the steps a pathogen must complete to cause an infection and then spread to a new host.
questions.explanation: Reservoir → transmission (contact, vehicle, or vector) → portal of entry (broken skin, mucous membranes, parenteral) → adherence → avoid host defenses → host damage → portal of exit (usually the same as entry), after which the host becomes a reservoir.
